articles.body: I Reopened My Own APK in JADX After Hardening It I develop Android applications that include authorization and payment functionality. Before every release, I have a habit of opening the release APK in JADX and searching through the package names. It started as a way to check whether obfuscation had missed anything. Eventually, it became a reason to worry about my own code. In the unprotected version, searching for an authorization class name immediately found it. I could expand a payment callback and read its implementation. String constants were still in plaintext. Obfuscation had changed some local variable names, but that did little to stop someone who understood the business logic.

articles.title: Why Your LLM City Map Collapses Without Spatial Constraints
articles.excerpt: The Problem When you prompt an LLM to "generate a map of an imaginary city with districts, roads, and landmarks," the initial output may appear plausible at first glance. Zoom in, however, and the geo…
articles.body: The Problem When you prompt an LLM to "generate a map of an imaginary city with districts, roads, and landmarks," the initial output may appear plausible at first glance. Zoom in, however, and the geometry collapses. Roads end abruptly at buildings. Districts overlap in ways that defy physical reality. Landmarks float in impossible positions—above mountains, inside lakes, or disconnected from their claimed terrain. The model has no internal sense of space; it simply generates tokens left to right, top to bottom, without maintaining any coordinate system. This is not merely a matter of occasional hallucination. It is a structural limitation baked into the autoregressive architecture.
articles.author: RobustTrueTry

articles.title: RS232 vs RS485 in a Vehicle: Which Serial Port for Which Peripheral
articles.excerpt: RS232 and RS485 both turn up on the same vehicle-terminal spec sheet, and integrators routinely wire the wrong one. The choice is not about speed or age. It comes down to two questions: how many devic…
articles.body: RS232 and RS485 both turn up on the same vehicle-terminal spec sheet, and integrators routinely wire the wrong one. The choice is not about speed or age. It comes down to two questions: how many devices are on the line, and how far does the cable run? The actual difference: single-ended vs differential RS232 sends each signal as a voltage measured against a shared ground. That works over a short cable in a quiet electrical environment. RS485 sends over a twisted pair and reads the difference between the two wires. Interference that hits the cable hits both wires roughly equally, and cancels out when the receiver subtracts one from the other. Distance, device count and noise immunity all follow from that one design difference.
articles.author: CF-Device

articles.title: Architecting a Low-Power Geofencing Engine: Lessons from Battery Optimization in Muffle
articles.excerpt: It was the second time that week. I was sitting in the back row of a lecture hall when my phone decided to announce my presence to the entire room with a high-pitched ringtone. It was a call from a re…
articles.body: It was the second time that week. I was sitting in the back row of a lecture hall when my phone decided to announce my presence to the entire room with a high-pitched ringtone. It was a call from a recruiter, and in my rush to silence the device, I fumbled the lock screen, accidentally declining the call and leaving the ringer volume cranked to maximum. The embarrassment was immediate and sharp. I looked around, feeling every pair of eyes on me, wishing I had just left the phone in my bag or, better yet, that it had known exactly where I was. That recurring frustration is the foundation of Muffle. We live in an era of context-aware computing, yet our phones remain stubbornly "dumb" when it comes to the simple task of respecting our environment.
articles.author: Haseeb

articles.title: With 160 skills installed, Claude Code kept 20 descriptions, and the model found 0 of 3 skills that lost theirs
articles.excerpt: With Opus 5.5's 1M-token window, Claude Code 2.1.289 held the skill listing to 30,000 characters. Of 160 project skills with 1,000-character descriptions, 20 kept their descriptions (22 of 40, 21 of 8…
articles.body: With Opus 5.5's 1M-token window, Claude Code 2.1.289 held the skill listing to 30,000 characters. Of 160 project skills with 1,000-character descriptions, 20 kept their descriptions (22 of 40, 21 of 80) and every name stayed, but the model invoked 0 of 3 target skills that were listed by name only, against 7 of 7 that still had descriptions. Every skill you install adds a line to the model's context on every turn: the skill's name and its description. When the model decides on its own whether a request calls for a skill, the description is all it has to go on.

articles.title: I turned a dead 4 GB laptop into a Matrix cyber-lab
articles.excerpt: I had an old laptop gathering dust. An 11-inch thing with 4 GB of RAM, a weak little CPU, and no graphics card. The kind of machine the internet tells you is e-waste. I made it my cyber-lab instead. H…
articles.body: I had an old laptop gathering dust. An 11-inch thing with 4 GB of RAM, a weak little CPU, and no graphics card . The kind of machine the internet tells you is e-waste. I made it my cyber-lab instead. Here's how it looks and what it actually does, because "old and slow" turned out to mean "perfect for learning without fear of breaking anything." Zero GPU. Zero dollars. Zero excuses. Make it look the part If you're going to learn Linux and cybersecurity, the machine might as well feel like it. So I gave it the full green-on-black treatment, all generated with Python, all free: A raccoon cursor. A normal arrow with a tiny raccoon riding along behind it. It's a real X cursor theme, so the whole desktop uses it. A live Matrix wallpaper. Falling green code that actually moves.

articles.title: 9 Legend of Zelda Side Quests Scarier than Any Horror Game
articles.excerpt: Cursed spider families, a ship that sails only at night, and a mummified father in a closet: nine Zelda side quests that belong in a horror story
articles.body: The Legend of Zelda has never been particularly shy about depicting curses, ghosts, and the walking dead (or ReDead). Its optional side quests are where Nintendo tends to let all three run wild. The series has always worked this way — usually giving you a bright, whimsical surface to explore with something rotten and/or horrifying tucked away, should you decide to look under that friendly surface. In the main story, that dread hides inside dungeons and boss fights. In the side quests, the dread has moved into the house next door, where it’s a bit more startling to discover. Curious what nightmares are hiding for Link throughout his various adventures? Check all the closets in the basement, first. Then read on, if you dare.
articles.author: Rebecca Corgan

articles.title: Animals Review
articles.excerpt: The new Netflix thriller Animals is tautly directed by Ben Affleck, who keeps the emphasis on the characters’ flawed humanity. None of the choices available to the protagonists are good ones, and the…
articles.body: Animals is in select theaters and on Netflix on October 9. Ben Affleck is back behind and in front of the camera with Animals, an entertaining new thriller that spices up the kidnap movie formula with a neat twist that asks big moral questions of its protagonists and viewers. Affleck plays Mark Kimball, a tycoon running as an independent candidate to become the next mayor of Los Angeles. (It should be noted that LA is currently in a heated mayoral campaign, so kudos, Netflix, on the timing of your film’s release.) Mark is a middle-aged white male Army veteran with progressive views and a Black wife and mixed-race son, who takes no outside funding and speaks fluent Spanish. It’s a cynical political strategist’s dream candidate come true, something the film acknowledges.
